chapters.title: The Feasts and Jesus
chapters.subtitle: How the New Testament reads Israel's calendar in the light of Jesus
chapters.nutshell: The New Testament writers were Jews who lived by Israel's calendar. When they told the story of Jesus they kept pointing to the feasts: the Passover lamb, the firstfruits, the gift of Pentecost, the Day of Atonement, the booths and lights of Sukkot.
chapters.bigIdea: The feasts do not disappear in Jesus; the New Testament sees him as filling them with their fullest meaning.
skeleton: Holy Week inside the Passover week

p: Jesus was circumcised, kept the Sabbath, went up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts and died at Passover. The Gospels often date events by the feasts (John 2:13; 5:1; 7:2; 10:22; 12:1). The chapter on the Jewish year explains what each feast is; here we ask how the New Testament connects each one with Jesus.

These links are not a code laid over the Bible from outside. Jesus and his first followers already lived inside these stories, and they used them to explain who he was and what his death and resurrection meant.

John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29). Jesus gives the Passover bread and cup a new meaning at his last supper (Luke 22:14–20). John notes that none of his bones were broken, like the Passover lamb (John 19:36; Exod 12:46), and Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7).

Paul turns Unleavened Bread into a picture of a cleansed life, "the bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:8). Firstfruits, the first sheaf of the barley harvest given to God, becomes a picture of the resurrection: Christ is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20–23) — the first of a great harvest.

sections.h: Shavuot: from Sinai to the Spirit
p: Fifty days after Passover came Shavuot (Weeks), called Pentecost in Greek. Jewish tradition links it with the giving of the Torah at Sinai, which came in the third month after the Exodus (Exod 19:1). In Acts 2 the Spirit is given on this very day, with wind and fire that recall Sinai.

Many readers notice a striking contrast. After the golden calf, about 3,000 people died (Exod 32:28); at Pentecost about 3,000 were added and given new life (Acts 2:41). Paul makes a similar contrast: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Cor 3:6).

The New Testament speaks of a trumpet sounding when Christ returns and the dead are raised (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52). Many Christians connect this with the Feast of Trumpets, though the texts do not name the feast. Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement through Jesus: he is the high priest who enters the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all (Heb 9:7–14, 24–28).

Sukkot is everywhere in John. The Word "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14). At this feast Jesus cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37–39), during the water-pouring days, and said, "I am the light of the world" (8:12) in the season of the great Temple lamps. Zechariah pictured all nations keeping Sukkot (Zech 14:16).

Hanukkah, the feast of Dedication, remembers the cleansing of the Temple in 164 BC. Jesus walked in Solomon's porch at this feast "and it was winter" (John 10:22–39). There he called himself the one "whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world" (10:36) — a fitting word at the feast of consecration and lights.

Purim, which celebrates God's rescue of the Jews in the story of Esther, has no direct link in the New Testament. Some have guessed that the unnamed "feast of the Jews" in John 5:1 was Purim, but this cannot be shown. It is honest to say that not every feast has a New Testament fulfilment.

sections.h: A popular pattern — held with care
p: Many Christians say that the spring feasts (Passover to Pentecost) were fulfilled at Jesus' first coming, and the autumn feasts (Trumpets, Atonement, Booths) point to his return. This is a common Christian reading and can be helpful, but the New Testament never sets it out as a scheme. Hebrews, for example, applies the Day of Atonement to the cross, not only to the future.
It is also good to remember that Jews keep these feasts today with their own rich meanings. Christians can learn from them with respect, rather than treating them as only shadows.

diagrams.title: Holy Week set against the Passover calendar
diagrams.note: Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper as the Passover meal (Mark 14:12); John places the crucifixion on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were slain (John 19:14). Scholars explain this difference in several ways; the dates below are a common reconstruction, not certain.

In the week of Firstfruits: "Christ the firstfruits" (1 Cor 15:20).

diagrams.title: From Passover to Pentecost: one story

steps.d: Passover: Jesus dies as the Lamb of God (John 1:29; 19:36).
Unleavened Bread: a people cleansed to live in sincerity and truth (1 Cor 5:7–8).
Firstfruits: Jesus raised as the first of the harvest (1 Cor 15:20).
Counting the days, as Israel counted from Passover to Shavuot (Lev 23:15–16; Acts 1:3).
Shavuot: as Sinai gave the Torah, Pentecost brings the Spirit who writes it on hearts (Acts 2; Jer 31:33).
Autumn feasts: many Christians see them pointing to his return — a reading held with humility.

verses.text: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.
Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

keyPoints: Jesus lived, taught and died within Israel's calendar of feasts.
Passover, Unleavened Bread and Firstfruits frame his death, burial and resurrection.
Pentecost was Shavuot, linked in Jewish tradition with Sinai; the Spirit was given that day.
Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement through Jesus; John is full of Sukkot and Hanukkah.
"Spring feasts at his first coming, autumn feasts at his return" is a common reading, not a New Testament rule.

chapters.title: How Prophecy Points to the Messiah
chapters.subtitle: What "Messiah" meant, how the New Testament reads the prophets, and how Jewish tradition reads them
chapters.nutshell: "Messiah" means "anointed one". In Jesus' day Jews hoped for different anointed figures. The New Testament reads the Old Testament in several ways — direct prediction, repeated patterns, and Israel's whole story reaching its goal — while Jewish tradition often reads the same texts differently.
chapters.bigIdea: The New Testament claims that Jesus fills up the whole story of Scripture, not only a handful of predictions.
skeleton: Three ways the New Testament reads prophecy
How Jewish tradition reads key texts

p: The Hebrew *mashiach* means "anointed one" — someone marked with oil for a task given by God. Kings were anointed (Saul is "the LORD's anointed", 1 Sam 24:6), and so were priests (Lev 4:3) and at least one prophet (1 Kgs 19:16). Even the Persian king Cyrus is called God's anointed (Isa 45:1). The Greek word is *christos*, so "Christ" is a title, not a surname.

sections.h: What Jews hoped for in Jesus' day
p: Hopes were varied. Many longed for a king from David's family who would drive out the nations and rule in justice; the Psalms of Solomon 17 (first century BC) describes such a "son of David". Some expected a prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15; John 1:21; 6:14). Some Dead Sea texts seem to speak of two anointed figures, a priestly one and a royal one (Community Rule 1QS 9:11) — scholars discuss exactly what they meant.

So when people asked, "Are you the Christ?", they did not all mean the same thing. Jesus often spoke of himself as "the Son of Man" instead, and filled the title with suffering as well as glory (Mark 8:29–31).

The New Testament does not read every text in the same way. Some texts are read as direct predictions (Mic 5:2 for Bethlehem). Others are patterns: Matthew quotes "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15), which in Hosea speaks of Israel leaving Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus reliving Israel's story, not Hosea forecasting an event. Rachel weeping (Jer 31:15; Matt 2:18) works the same way.

The Greek verb for "fulfil", *plēroō*, means "to fill full". Jesus fills Scripture full, like a pattern finally complete. Jesus himself said he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them (Matt 5:17).

On the road to Emmaus Jesus began "with Moses and all the Prophets" and explained what was said about himself in all the Scriptures (Luke 24:27). Later he named the three parts of the Hebrew Bible: "the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms" (24:44). The Old Testament verse quoted or echoed most often in the New is usually said to be Psalm 110:1, "The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand."

sections.h: How Jewish tradition reads these texts
p: Jewish tradition also reads many texts as messianic. The Aramaic Targum on Isaiah 52:13 says, "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper", though it applies the sufferings mostly to others. Later commentators, such as Rashi in the eleventh century, read Isaiah 53 as describing the people of Israel. The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) speaks of a Messiah son of Joseph who is slain and a Messiah son of David — how old this idea is remains debated.

Many Jews did not and do not accept Jesus as Messiah, for serious reasons: the expected age of peace, the return of the exiles and a rebuilt Temple are not yet seen (Isa 2:4); a crucified Messiah seemed impossible (1 Cor 1:23); and Christian teaching about Jesus' divinity seems to them to clash with God's oneness. Sadly, centuries of Christian mistreatment of Jews also made the message harder to hear.

diagrams.title: Three ways the New Testament reads prophecy

steps.d: A text looks ahead to a future event. Example: a ruler from Bethlehem (Mic 5:2 → Matt 2:6).
An earlier person or event shows a shape that is repeated more fully. Example: Israel, God's son, called out of Egypt (Hos 11:1 → Matt 2:15).
Israel's whole story — exodus, exile, return — reaches its goal in Jesus. Example: Rachel's weeping and the hope after it (Jer 31:15–17 → Matt 2:18).
"Fulfil" means "fill full" — not only a prediction ticked off, but a pattern brought to completion (Matt 5:17; Luke 24:44).

diagrams.title: Four texts: Christian and Jewish readings
diagrams.note: Both sides contain a range of views; these are common readings, simplified.

left.label: Common Christian reading
items: Isaiah 53: the suffering Servant is Jesus, who bears the sins of many (Acts 8:32–35).
Psalm 110:1: David calls the Messiah "my Lord"; Jesus is seated at God's right hand (Mark 12:36).
Isaiah 7:14: the virgin-born child is Jesus, "God with us" (Matt 1:23).
Zechariah 12:10: "they will look on him whom they pierced" — Jesus on the cross (John 19:37).

right.label: Common Jewish reading
items: Isaiah 53: the Servant is Israel suffering among the nations (Rashi); the Targum calls the Servant the Messiah but shifts the suffering.
Psalm 110:1: about Abraham or David as God's chosen king; some sources also read it of the Messiah.
Isaiah 7:14: a young woman (*almah*) in King Ahaz's day; the child is a sign for that time.
Zechariah 12:10: the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) applies it to a slain Messiah son of Joseph; others to those killed in battle.

verses.text: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus…
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
I have not come to abolish them but to fulfil them.
The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."

keyPoints: Mashiach means "anointed"; kings, priests and even Cyrus were called anointed.
Jewish hopes in Jesus' day were varied: a Davidic king, a prophet like Moses, perhaps a priestly figure.
The New Testament reads prophecy as prediction, as pattern, and as Israel's story filled full.
Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament verse the New Testament uses most.
Jewish tradition reads many of the same texts differently, for serious reasons that deserve respect.

chapters.title: Key Messianic Prophecies
chapters.subtitle: Twenty promises — what they said then, how Jews read them, and how the New Testament sees Jesus in them
chapters.nutshell: The New Testament quotes many Old Testament promises about a coming king, prophet, priest and servant. Each one first spoke into its own time. Reading the setting, the Jewish reading and the New Testament use side by side helps us see both the meaning and the claim.
chapters.bigIdea: Messianic prophecies are best read in three steps: their first setting, how Jewish readers heard them, and how the New Testament sees them filled full in Jesus.
skeleton: The Law, the kings and the Psalms

p: When you meet a "messianic prophecy", ask three questions. What did it mean in its first setting? How have Jewish readers understood it? How does the New Testament use it? Many promises spoke first to a king or crisis in Israel's own day, and were later seen to have a larger meaning. That does not weaken them; it shows how God's story builds.

sections.h: The Law, the kings and the Psalms
p: The first set of cards begins in Genesis with the promise that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent, and the sceptre of Judah. It moves through the prophet like Moses and God's covenant with David, to the royal psalms where the king is God's "son", is kept from the grave, cries "My God, my God" and sits at God's right hand.

The second set gathers Isaiah's sign of Immanuel, the child with royal names, the suffering Servant and the anointed preacher of good news; Daniel's "son of man"; Micah's ruler from Bethlehem; and Zechariah's humble king and the one who was pierced. Other key promises — Abraham's blessing to the nations, the shoot from Jesse, the righteous Branch and the messenger of Malachi — appear in the table.

Some texts are debated. In Isaiah 7:14 the Hebrew *almah* means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Septuagint chose *parthenos*, usually "virgin", which Matthew quotes (Matt 1:23). Jews read the sign as given to King Ahaz; Christians see a fuller meaning in Jesus' birth. In Psalm 22:16 most Hebrew manuscripts read "like a lion, my hands and feet", while the Septuagint has "they dug (pierced)"; a Dead Sea copy may support a verb. Both points are honestly discussed by scholars.

Some promises are close to direct predictions: a ruler from Bethlehem, a humble king on a donkey. Others are patterns: the suffering righteous one of Psalm 22, the king of Psalm 2. The New Testament uses both. Its deepest claim is not that Jesus matched a list, but that in him the whole hope of Israel — king, prophet, priest and servant — comes together.

diagrams.title: The Law, the kings and the Psalms

cards.front: Genesis 3:15: the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head.
cards.back: After the fall God promises lasting conflict between the serpent and the woman's offspring; the serpent strikes the heel, but its head is crushed.
cards.source: Early Targums speak of healing for this wound "in the days of King Messiah".
cards.echo: Satan crushed under your feet (Rom 16:20); born of a woman (Gal 4:4); destroying the devil (Heb 2:14).

cards.front: Genesis 49:10: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah.
cards.back: Jacob blesses Judah with lasting rule "until Shiloh comes" or "until he comes to whom it belongs" — the Hebrew is hard.
cards.source: The Targum Onkelos reads: "until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs".
cards.echo: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Rev 5:5); our Lord came from Judah (Heb 7:14).

cards.front: Deuteronomy 18:15–18: God will raise up a prophet like Moses.
cards.back: God promises to keep speaking through prophets, so Israel need not turn to diviners. Yet no prophet arose like Moses (Deut 34:10).
cards.source: Jews in Jesus' day waited for "the Prophet" (John 1:21); Samaritans hoped for a Moses-like figure.
cards.echo: Peter applies it to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23); "Listen to him" (Matt 17:5); John 6:14.

cards.front: 2 Samuel 7:12–16: your throne shall be established forever.
cards.back: God promises David a son who will build the Temple and a dynasty that lasts; "I will be his father, and he shall be my son". It speaks first of Solomon (7:13–14).
cards.source: The root of the Jewish hope for a "son of David" (Psalms of Solomon 17).
cards.echo: "The throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32–33); "I will be to him a father" (Heb 1:5).

cards.front: Psalm 2:7: "You are my son; today I have begotten you."
cards.back: A coronation psalm: on the day the king of David's line is crowned, God adopts him as his son and gives him the nations.
cards.source: Read of the Davidic king; ancient Jewish writings also applied it to the Messiah (Psalms of Solomon 17 echoes Ps 2:9).
cards.echo: The voice at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:11); applied to the resurrection (Acts 13:33; Heb 1:5).

cards.front: Psalm 16:10: you will not abandon my soul to Sheol.
cards.back: David trusts God to keep him from death; the Greek translation says God will not let his holy one "see corruption".
cards.source: Read as David's confidence in God's protection.
cards.echo: Peter: David died, but Christ was raised and did not see corruption (Acts 2:25–31; 13:35).

cards.front: Psalm 22: forsaken, mocked, hands and feet attacked, clothes divided.
cards.back: A righteous sufferer cries out (22:1), is surrounded by enemies (22:16), sees his clothes shared out (22:18), then praises God before the nations (22:22–31). Verse 16 reads "like a lion" in most Hebrew copies and "they pierced" in the Septuagint.
cards.source: Read of David, or of Israel in its sufferings.
cards.echo: Jesus prays 22:1 on the cross (Mark 15:34); the clothes divided (John 19:24); Heb 2:12 quotes 22:22.

cards.front: Psalm 110:1, 4: "Sit at my right hand… a priest forever."
cards.back: A royal psalm: God enthrones David's lord and makes him a priest "after the order of Melchizedek", king and priest together.
cards.source: Some Jewish sources read it of Abraham or of David; others of the Messiah.
cards.echo: Jesus asks how David's son is David's Lord (Mark 12:35–37); Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 5–7.

cards.front: Isaiah 7:14: the almah will conceive and bear a son, Immanuel.
cards.back: A sign to King Ahaz (c. 735 BC): before the child knows right from wrong, the two kings threatening Judah will be gone (7:16).
cards.source: Jewish readers see a young woman and a child of Ahaz's time; almah means young woman, the Greek parthenos usually "virgin".
cards.echo: Matthew sees the sign filled full in Jesus' virgin birth: "God with us" (Matt 1:22–23).

cards.front: Isaiah 9:6–7: Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
cards.back: After darkness in Galilee (9:1–2) a royal child is born who will sit on David's throne with justice and endless peace.
cards.source: Often read of King Hezekiah; the Targum speaks of the Messiah "in whose days peace will increase".
cards.echo: Light dawns in Galilee (Matt 4:15–16); the throne of David (Luke 1:32–33).

cards.back: The Servant is despised, bears others' sins like a guilt offering, dies, and is then exalted and "sees offspring".
cards.source: The Targum: "my servant the Messiah", with the suffering shifted to others; Rashi and many later commentators: Israel.
cards.echo: Philip explains it to the Ethiopian (Acts 8:32–35); 1 Pet 2:22–25; Matt 8:17; Luke 22:37.

cards.front: Isaiah 61:1–2: the Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me.
cards.back: An anointed messenger proclaims release to captives and "the year of the LORD's favour", Jubilee language for the returning exiles.
cards.source: Dead Sea texts (11QMelchizedek; 4Q521) use these words of an end-time deliverer.
cards.echo: Jesus reads it in Nazareth: "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled" (Luke 4:18–21).

cards.t: One like a son of man
cards.front: Daniel 7:13–14: coming with the clouds, given everlasting dominion.
cards.back: After four beast-empires, a human figure is brought to the Ancient of Days and given the kingdom; it is shared with "the saints" (7:18, 27).
cards.source: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) reads it of the Messiah; some read the figure as Israel itself.
cards.echo: Jesus before the high priest: "you will see the Son of Man… coming with the clouds" (Mark 14:62).

cards.front: Micah 5:2: from you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, will come a ruler.
cards.back: In a time of Assyrian threat, Micah promises a new David from David's own small town, "whose origins are from of old".
cards.source: The Targum: "from you shall come forth before me the Messiah"; the scribes in Matthew read it the same way.

cards.front: Zechariah 9:9: your king comes, righteous, humble, riding on a donkey.
cards.back: After the exile, a king of peace comes to Zion, not on a war horse; he speaks peace to the nations (9:10).
cards.source: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) reads it of the Messiah, coming humbly if Israel is unworthy.
cards.echo: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey (Matt 21:4–5; John 12:14–15).

cards.front: Zechariah 12:10: they will look on me, whom they have pierced, and mourn.
cards.back: God pours out a spirit of grace on Jerusalem, and the people mourn as for an only son.
cards.source: The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) links it to the slain Messiah son of Joseph.
cards.echo: "They will look on him whom they have pierced" (John 19:37; Rev 1:7).

diagrams.title: Twenty promises at a glance
diagrams.note: Dates are approximate; some are debated. "Pattern" means a text that first spoke of its own time and is seen as filled full in Jesus.

cells: Isaiah; many scholars date to 6th c. BC
Isaiah; many scholars date to 6th c. BC
The righteous Branch; our righteousness (1 Cor 1:30)

places.d: David's town; Micah promised a ruler from here.
Jesus' home town; here he read Isaiah 61 and said it was fulfilled.
John baptised here as the messenger who prepares the way.
In Galilee of the nations, where Isaiah saw a great light dawning.
Near the Mount of Olives; from here Jesus rode into Jerusalem.
City of David's throne and of the Temple; the king's entry, the cross and the pierced one.
Where David was first anointed king, the start of the royal line.

verses.text: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah… from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.
But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities.
Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey.
Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

keyPoints: Read each prophecy first in its own setting.
Many Jewish sources also read these texts as messianic, though often differently.
Some texts are predictions; others are patterns filled full in Jesus.
Hard texts like Isaiah 7:14 and Psalm 22:16 should be discussed honestly.
The New Testament sees king, prophet, priest and servant come together in Jesus.

quiz.why: Luke 4:18–21: "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled."

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew almah in Isaiah 7:14 mean?
quiz.why: Almah means a young woman; the Greek Septuagint chose parthenos, usually "virgin".

quiz.q: Which text does the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) apply to a slain Messiah son of Joseph?
quiz.why: Sukkah 52a links the mourning of Zechariah 12:10 to Messiah son of Joseph.

terms.def: Hebrew for a young woman of marriageable age (Isa 7:14).
